title: Stage wagon
wikitext:
{{Short description|Light horse-drawn public passenger vehicle}} {{Use mdy dates|date=May 2026}} {{for|the mobile platforms used to support and transport scenery on theater stages|Scenery wagon}} [[File:Woolaroc - Postkutsche.jpg|thumb|An Overland wagon]] [[File:Photograph of a stage coach. The coach is a "mudwagon" used to travel through rugged terrain. - NARA - 296584 (cropped).jpg|thumb|A mud-wagon]] '''Stage wagons''', also called '''passenger wagons''' or '''mud wagons''', were [[horse-drawn vehicle|horse-drawn]] public passenger vehicles used on early stage lines, and were predecessors of the larger and more comfortable [[stagecoach]]. Designed for rough or muddy terrain, they were lighter and more rugged than stagecoaches and were commonly used where poor roads or low passenger demand did not justify operating a full-sized coach. In the early American West, a [[U.S. Mail]] contract was considered the "life-blood of the staging industry", providing the revenue needed to sustain stage lines. Many western routes began with stage wagons, and operators often continued using them even after the more expensive stagecoaches became available.{{r|KW}} == Design and variations == [[File:Butterfield's Stage (Celerity) Wagon.jpg|thumb|This drawing illustrates the typical suspension method of a stage wagon]] The early English freight wagon style of stage wagon had double shafts for wheelers, well-dished wheels with wide treads, and a canvas top over bows. They were very heavy and difficult to overturn, unsprung, lumbering, and driven at a walk. The later American stage wagon had {{Glossary link|glossary=Glossary of carriage and driving terminology|thoroughbraces}}, sprung seats, a canvas top on {{Glossary link|glossary=Glossary of carriage and driving terminology|pillar}}s, and a luggage compartment on the back.{{r|smith|p=153}}{{r|berkebile1978|pp=211, 258,262}} Passenger wagons had several crosswise bench seats inside; in America seats were sometimes mounted on springs. Different designs accommodated from 4 to 12 passengers. Early models had the driver's seat inside with the passengers, and passengers had to climb over the driver's seat to get inside. Later models had door openings, but no doors, and the driver's seat was moved outside the main compartment. American stage wagons had 6-8 permanent pillars and a flat canvas top or a permanent solid top. The sides were open; some models had roll-down curtains for inclement weather. The wagon was designed as a box on curved sills. Early models were unsprung, but later a low thoroughbrace suspension was added, attached lower than the high thoroughbrace arcs seen on the later [[Concord coach]]es.{{r|smith|p=153}}{{r|berkebile1978|pp=211, 258,262}} Some models were named "Overland", many of which were built by [[Abbot-Downing Company]].{{r|smith|p=126}}{{r|berkebile1978|p=210}} The Celerity wagon was created for [[Butterfield Overland Mail]].{{r|KW}}{{r|smith|p=41}}{{r|berkebile1978|p=80}} The term ''mud wagon'' was used for vehicles similar to the [[Concord coach]] but of inferior class, lighter, smaller, and with minimal weather protection for passengers. {{r|smith|p=120}}{{r|berkebile1978|p=200}} File:At Long Island Museum 2025 072.jpg|1870 passenger wagon, Abbot-Downing Company File:Abbot, Downing 1871 catalog Chart A1.jpg|[[Abbot-Downing Company|Abbot, Downing's]] ''Overland Wagon''
a canvas-topped stage wagon 1871{{efn|available in two sizes, 6 or 9 passengers and available with: doors, painted sail duck top, sail duck or enameled curtains, lined in leather, back boot, driver's apron. Abbot, Downing & Co. catalog 1871}} File:Grabill - The Deadwood Coach-1.jpg|Two large Overland stage wagons on the road to [[Pierre, South Dakota]] in 1889. File:Grabill - The last Deadwood Coach-2.jpg|December 28, 1890. The last Deadwood stage == Historical context == [[File:Hammond Tenterden.jpg|thumb|Trade card of R Hammond of Tenterden, 1750. Freight {{convert|65|mi|km}} to [[Southwark]] at the south end of [[London Bridge]] from [[Tenterden]] in the [[Kentish Weald]] and return, once each week]] Wagons carrying freight had been taking passengers in Europe since 1500. This particular stage wagon type was first recorded near the end of the 18th century in use in eastern North America, US and Upper and Lower Canada. It was an unsprung wagon with the driver's bench seat providing room for two more passengers beside him. It might also carry more passenger seats on the tray behind. These extra seats were reached by climbing over the driver's seat. About this time, the Postmaster General [[Joseph Habersham]] required the driver's seat to be moved from the tray onto a front wall to improve the driver's vision and by dropping the tray improve the wagon's stability. This created the characteristic stagecoach-like profile of the stage wagon. Their relatively simple design and construction allowed them to be sold by [[Abbot-Downing Company|Abbot, Downing]] at around half the price of full-size [[Concord coach]]es. Their suspension employed thoroughbraces that were much shorter than those used on Concord stagecoaches. {{clear}} == Manufacturers == Some of the known manufacturers of stage wagons include: * [[Abbot-Downing Company|Abbot, Downing]], [[Concord, New Hampshire]] * Milton P Henderson of [[Stockton California]] made stage wagons of the same style as Abbot, Downing. The firm began in 1869 as a partnership with E G Clark. They can be identified by the finish of the sides of the bodies and the method of attachment of iron stays back and front. * P O LeMay and Livy Swan at [[Yreka, California]] * Weisenhorn Carriage in [[Helena, Montana]] built a vehicle very like an Abbot, Downing ''Australian wagon'' * Celerity was a brand of Stage wagon made in [[Troy, New York]]. ==Notes== {{Notelist}} == See also == * [[Stagecoach]] * [[Concord coach]] == References == {{Cite book |last=Berkebile |first=Donald H. |title=Carriage Terminology: An Historical Dictionary |year=1978 |publisher=Smithsonian Institution Scholarly Press |isbn=9781935623434 |ol=4534466M}} {{Cite magazine |first=Ken |last=Wheeling |title=They Called Them Mudders |magazine=[[The Carriage Journal]] |volume=43 |issue=5 |date=October 2005 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Carriage_Journal/8cREDwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=The%20Carriage%20Journal%3A%20Vol%2043%20No%205%20October%202005&pg=PA236&printsec=frontcover |pages=236ff}} {{cite book |title=A Dictionary of Horse Drawn Vehicles |first=D.J.M. |last=Smith |year=1988 |publisher=J.
